CORS flow in reading the ResponsesEvery developer meets CORS the same way: an error in the console, a lost afternoon, and a Stack Overflow answer that says app.use(cors({ origin: "*" })). The error disappears. You move on. You never actually learn what happened.
Here’s the sentence that fixes it:
CORS doesn’t block your request. The request goes through. CORS blocks your JavaScript from reading the response.
If that surprises you, keep reading. Five minutes and it will click for good.

The rule underneath it: Same-Origin Policy
Browsers enforce one hard rule by default: JavaScript can only read responses from its own origin.
An origin is scheme + host + port, all three must match:
https://myapp.com vs http://myapp.com ❌ scheme
https://myapp.com vs https://api.myapp.com ❌ host
https://myapp.com vs https://myapp.com:3000 ❌ portChange any one, and it’s a different origin. Your JS is blocked from reading the response. By default. With zero configuration.
Why this rule has to exist
Imagine it didn’t. You’re logged into your bank in one tab. You open a sketchy site in another:
// running on evil.com, while you're logged into your bank elsewhere
const res = await fetch("https://yourbank.com/api/account", {
credentials: "include" // attach my bank cookies 🍪
});
const data = await res.json(); // 💀 evil.com just read your balance
sendToAttacker(data);The browser automatically attaches your bank cookie to any request going to the bank it doesn’t care which site’s code started it. The cookie follows the destination, not the sender.
So without the Same-Origin Policy, any website’s JavaScript could ride on your live logins and read your private data everywhere. That’s the catastrophe SOP prevents. It blocks evil.com from reading the bank’s response automatically, out of the box.

So what is CORS, then?
Here’s the reframe most tutorials miss.
SOP is the wall. It blocks everything cross-origin by default. CORS is the gate you install in that wall for origins you trust.
You don’t configure CORS to block attackers — they’re already blocked. You configure it to allow your own frontend through:
app.use(cors({
origin: "https://myapp.com", // 👈 let MY frontend read responses
credentials: true
}));That’s not adding protection. That’s granting an exception. evil.com stays blocked because you simply never added it to the list.
Server declares who’s allowed (via a header). Browser enforces it. The server is the bouncer writing the guest list. The browser is the doorman checking it.
The header that does it:
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://myapp.comNo matching header → browser blocks the read → CORS error in your console.

The mind-bender: the request already happened
This is the part that reframes everything.
1. Your JS calls the API
2. Browser SENDS the request ← it goes out
3. Server processes it, responds ← the work is DONE
4. Browser checks the Allow-Origin header
✅ match → your JS reads the response
❌ no match → browser blocks the READ, throws a CORS errorStep 3 already ran. If the call was POST /delete-account, the account is gone. CORS only stopped your JavaScript from reading the reply.
The server did the work. The browser just refused to hand your code the result.

Why “it works in Postman but not the browser”
Because CORS is a browser feature. It does not exist anywhere else.
Browser: send → receive → 🚦 check CORS header → maybe block the read
Postman: send → receive → ✅ show you everything. No gatekeeper.Postman isn’t ignoring CORS or bypassing it. There’s simply no Same-Origin Policy to enforce Postman isn’t a browser. Same for curl, and same for your backend calling another backend. Server-to-server calls have no CORS. Ever.
The practical payoff: when you hit a CORS error, it’s never a bug in your request, and Postman can never help you debug it (it will always “work” there). The fix is always on the server sending the right header never in your frontend fetch call.

The credentials trap (the one that breaks auth)
If your request sends cookies, the rules get stricter:
fetch("https://api.myapp.com/me", { credentials: "include" })// server — BOTH now required:
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://myapp.com // ❗ EXACT origin, never "*"
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true // ❗ must be presentThe wildcard * is forbidden when credentials are involved. The browser flat-out refuses the combo. That's deliberate "allow any origin and send cookies" would rebuild the exact attack SOP was made to stop.
This single misconfiguration breaks more auth setups than anything else. If your login cookie won’t flow cross-origin, this is almost always why.

The mistake to never make
You hit a CORS error, panic, and reach for this:
app.use(cors({ origin: "*" })); // ❌ makes the error go awayYou think you’re being permissive. What you actually did was tear the gate off the wall for every site on the internet.
Even worse is reflecting the origin back:
res.header("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", req.headers.origin); // ❌ allows EVERYONEThat looks like “works with everything” because it literally allows every origin including evil.com while also permitting credentials. Always check an allowlist instead:
const allowed = ["https://myapp.com", "https://admin.myapp.com"];
if (allowed.includes(req.headers.origin))
res.header("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", req.headers.origin); // ✅The rule: wildcard * is safe only for public, unauthenticated resources a font, a public API keyed by a URL token. The moment a cookie is involved, exact allowlist only.

CORS is not protecting your server
Worth saying plainly: CORS protects your users’ browsers from other sites. It does nothing for your server.
Anyone can still hit your API with curl, Postman, or a script CORS never sees them. CORS is not authentication, not authorization, not a firewall. If an endpoint needs protecting, it needs real auth. CORS only governs what browser JavaScript on other origins can read.
And the flip side the thing CORS doesn’t stop look again at that attack:
// evil.com — doesn't care about reading the response
fetch("https://yourbank.com/api/transfer", {
method: "POST",
credentials: "include",
body: JSON.stringify({ to: "attacker", amount: 10000 })
});The request still fires. The cookie still attaches. The transfer might still execute. CORS blocked evil.com from reading the reply but the attacker never needed to read it. They just needed the action to happen.
That gap is CSRF, and it needs its own defense: SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens. CORS guards reads; CSRF protection guards writes. Neither replaces the other.

See it break in 30 seconds
Open the console on any website and run:
fetch("https://api.github.com/users/torvalds")
.then(r => r.json()).then(console.log); // ✅ works — GitHub sends Allow-Origin: *fetch("https://www.google.com")
.then(r => r.text()).then(console.log); // ❌ CORS error — no such headerWatch the second fail. Then open the Network tab and notice the impossible-looking thing:
The failed request has a status code. It completed. The response came back. The console shows a CORS error, but the Network tab shows the request finished.
That gap request succeeded, JS couldn’t read it is the entire concept of CORS in one screenshot.

The whole thing, locked in
❌ CORS controls what the browser SENDS
✅ CORS controls what your JS is allowed to READ❌ the browser decides who's allowed
✅ the server declares (header), the browser enforces❌ CORS blocks attackers
✅ SOP blocks attackers by default; CORS opens a gate for who you trustSOP is the wall. CORS is the gate. It guards the read, not the request — and it protects your users, not your server.
Get those three lines and you will never wildcard a CORS config in a panic again.

This is part of a series on the stuff we all use in web dev but rarely open up tokens, password hashing, and now CORS. Next: CSRF vs XSS, the exact attack CORS deliberately doesn’t stop.
What’s the longest you’ve ever spent debugging a CORS error that turned out to be one missing header? I once lost two hours to a trailing slash in the allowed origin. 🙃
